opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think inverse design is one of the most exciting frontiers for AI right now, because it flips the traditional engineering workflow on its head.

Historically, if you wanted to design something physical, like an airfoil, a medical device, or a new material, you'd propose a design, run an expensive simulation or build a prototype, look at the results, and iterate. Each loop could take hours or days on a supercomputer, so you'd explore only a tiny fraction of the possible design space. Inverse design asks the opposite question: given the behavior I want, what design gets me there?

The bottleneck has always been the cost of the forward model, the physics simulation. That's where neural operators come in. With Fourier neural operators and related architectures, we learn the solution operator of partial differential equations directly. They work across resolutions and can be orders of magnitude faster than traditional numerical solvers, sometimes a thousand times or more. Once you have a fast, differentiable surrogate for the physics, you can do gradient-based optimization over the design and explore far more candidates than was ever possible.

We've seen this play out concretely. One example I like is a medical catheter design. We used AI to redesign the internal geometry of a catheter to reduce bacterial contamination moving upstream, which is a major cause of hospital infections. The AI-optimized design reduced bacterial contamination dramatically in lab experiments, and it was 3D-printed and tested in the real world. That's the full loop: simulation, optimization, fabrication, validation.

There are similar opportunities in aerodynamics, fusion plasma modeling, weather and climate, carbon capture, and chip design. Anywhere you have expensive physics and a large design space, this approach can help.

A few things are important to get right. First, you need models that respect the physics. Purely data-driven models can hallucinate outputs that look plausible but violate conservation laws. So we combine data with physics constraints, what we call physics-informed operator learning, so the model stays grounded even outside its training data. Second, resolution invariance matters a lot, because real engineering problems are multi-scale and you want to train on coarse data and still predict fine-scale behavior. Third, you need to close the loop with experiments, because ultimately the physical world is the judge.

Longer term, I see this becoming a kind of AI scientist for engineering, where language models handle reasoning and planning, and neural operators handle the physical understanding that language alone can't capture. Text on the internet won't teach a model fluid dynamics; it has to learn from simulations and experiments. Bringing those together could compress design cycles from years to weeks, and that's where I think the biggest innovation gains will come from.

r001.rationale: It describes learning a fast, differentiable model of physical behavior and using it for gradient-based design optimization toward a desired behavior.

r002.rationale: It says expensive simulations limit how much of the design space can be explored, but does not identify highly nonlinear interactions or explain that they make manual design difficult.

r003.rationale: It describes simulating designs, examining results, and iterating, then identifies simulation as part of the AI design loop before fabrication and validation.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about inverse design is that it really flips the traditional engineering workflow on its head. For most of history, if you wanted to design a wing or a catheter or a new material, you'd start from a design, run a simulation or build a prototype, see how it performs, tweak it, and iterate. That loop is expensive, because the simulation itself, solving the underlying partial differential equations, might take hours or days on a supercomputer. So you can only afford a handful of iterations, and you end up with designs that are heavily constrained by what a human intuited at the start.

What AI lets us do is learn the solution operator of those physical systems. With neural operators, instead of solving the equations from scratch every time, we learn a mapping from the input, the geometry, the boundary conditions, to the output, the pressure field, the flow, the stress. And that learned model is differentiable and runs orders of magnitude faster. So now you can ask the question the other way around: here's the performance I want, what design gives me that? You take gradients through the model with respect to the shape itself, and you can search a design space that is far larger than anything a human would enumerate by hand.

A concrete example from our group is the catheter work. Bacterial contamination in catheters is a huge problem, and people had tried various geometries for the interior. We used a neural operator to model how bacteria swim upstream in the fluid, and then optimized the geometry directly. The result was a design with these asymmetric tooth-like structures that redirect the bacteria, and in experiments it reduced contamination by something like a hundredfold. Nobody sketched that shape. It came out of the optimization.

The same thing shows up in weather and climate with FourCastNet, in carbon capture with modeling plume dynamics underground, in nuclear fusion with controlling plasma. The common thread is that once simulation becomes cheap and differentiable, design stops being bottlenecked by compute and starts being bottlenecked by imagination and by how well we specify what we want.

I do want to be careful about the caveats. These models are only as good as the data and the physics you bake in, so we spend a lot of effort on things like physics-informed losses and making sure the models generalize across resolutions and out of the training distribution. And ultimately you still need to validate in the real world. But I think we're at the beginning of a period where the pace of innovation in physical systems, which has been so much slower than in software, can start to catch up. That's what excites me most.

r001.rationale: The response says a neural operator maps design inputs such as geometry and boundary conditions to physical outputs, then uses gradients through that model to optimize the geometry for desired performance.

r002.rationale: It says human intuition limits manual design, but does not identify highly nonlinear interactions as a reason people struggle to design physical systems.

r003.rationale: The response describes using the learned physical model to predict performance while optimizing geometry, and says the resulting design was validated in experiments.

astra-6.text:
What excites me about inverse design is that it changes where we start. Instead of choosing a design, simulating it, and then making adjustments, we can start with the properties we want and ask: what physical structure would achieve them? That could be an airfoil with lower drag, a material with particular thermal properties, or a device that operates efficiently under different conditions.

AI can make that search much faster. If we can learn a useful approximation of the underlying physics, we can explore many more candidates than we could by running an expensive simulation for each one. And we can search across a broader range of shapes and structures, potentially finding solutions that a human designer wouldn’t have considered.

But the key is to close the loop with physics and experiments. A design can look excellent according to a learned model and still fail when you manufacture it or test it outside the conditions the model has seen. So we need accurate validation, uncertainty estimates, and manufacturing constraints built into the process.

I see the opportunity as expanding what engineers can explore—while making the path from an idea to a validated physical system much faster.

r001.rationale: It describes starting from desired physical properties, asking what structure achieves them, and using a learned approximation of physics to search candidate designs.

r002.rationale: It says AI may find designs a human would not consider, but does not identify highly nonlinear interactions as a reason humans struggle to design systems manually.

r003.rationale: It calls for validation with physics and experiments, but does not explain that simulation within the AI design loop checks whether generated designs work.

sol-6.1.text:
What excites me about inverse design is that it changes where we start. Traditionally, you propose a design, simulate how it behaves, and then keep adjusting it. With inverse design, you start with the properties you want—say, an aircraft component that is lighter but still strong—and work backward toward a design that achieves them.

AI can make that process much faster by learning the relationship between designs and their physical behavior. Neural operators, for example, can learn mappings between functions, allowing us to approximate physical simulations efficiently and explore many more possibilities.

But speed alone isn’t enough. The designs have to obey the physics, be manufacturable, and work under conditions beyond the training data. So I see the most powerful approach as a loop: AI proposes candidates, physics-based simulation and experiments validate them, and those results improve the model. That can help us discover designs for materials, energy systems, and other physical technologies that would be difficult to find through conventional trial and error.

r001.rationale: It describes working backward from desired physical properties to a design and says AI learns the relationship between designs and physical behavior, approximating simulations to explore designs.

r002.rationale: It does not mention highly nonlinear interactions or say that they make manual design difficult.

r003.rationale: It says physics-based simulation and experiments validate AI-proposed candidates to check that designs work.
